subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage:
Monday: Raghav came back from his night shift at the call centre to find the sink full: Hemant's dal pot, three mugs, a frying pan with egg stuck to it. He washed his own plate around them and said nothing.
Wednesday: Same pile, taller. Raghav had also covered the electricity bill again, and Hemant still hadn't transferred his half.
Thursday: The pot was growing something. Hemant was on the sofa, headphones on, laughing at a video. Raghav stood at the sink and said, loud enough, "Wow. Maybe the dishes will wash themselves if we believe hard enough." His voice had an edge he didn't recognise. It wasn't really the pot. It was feeling like the only adult in the flat, like nobody saw what he did.

qa.q: What had Raghav covered again by Wednesday?
qa.a: He had covered the electricity bill again.

qa.q: What is Raghav really feeling behind the sarcastic remark?
qa.a: He feels unseen and resentful, like the only adult in the flat, covering the bill and the dishes while nobody notices what he does.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Raghav at this first spark?
qa.a: He could name the real issue calmly, such as "I'm feeling taken for granted with the dishes and the bill, can we set up a system?", instead of sarcasm.

qa.q: How might Hemant hear the remark from the sofa?
qa.a: Hemant may hear only mockery out of nowhere, not knowing about the bill or the build-up, and feel attacked rather than asked.

grounding: Shows a flatmate whose sarcastic line about days-old dishes really comes from a quietly growing sense of being disrespected.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage: Your grandfather Gurpreet was not always this patient, Madhuri. At twenty-one I shared two rooms in Ludhiana with a boy called Satnam, both of us new at the textile mill. Every evening I came home to his tea glasses on the floor and his socks on my chair. Third day in a row, I picked up a glass and said, very sweetly, "Thank you, Satnam ji, for decorating our home." He laughed. I didn't. Later, lying awake, I understood it had nothing to do with glasses. I had been cooking for both of us for a month, and he had never once said it was good. I felt like a servant, not a friend. That is what the remark was really about. So when you complain about your flatmate's dishes, ask yourself what you are actually hungry for.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet share rooms at twenty-one?
qa.a: He shared two rooms in Ludhiana with Satnam, both new at the textile mill.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet realise he was really feeling that night?
qa.a: He realised he felt like a servant, not a friend, because he had cooked for a month without one word of thanks.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet advise Madhuri to do before complaining about a flatmate?
qa.a: To ask what one is actually hungry for, meaning the need underneath the complaint, before speaking.

qa.q: Why might Satnam have laughed at the remark?
qa.a: Satnam probably heard only a joke about glasses and had no idea about the month of unthanked cooking building up underneath.

grounding: Shows a young man's sarcastic remark about mess that is really about feeling unappreciated, told by him as an elder.
